input: Recommendation: it is recommended that the plant run the sensor pilot on 18 pumps for three months, at a cost of $44k, and hold the decision on full installation until the pilot reports. The reliability engineering group will own the pilot and will report before the March capital review. According to the plant's maintenance records for 12 months, there were 1345 h of unplanned downtime across its 260 pumps, and bearing failures account for 45% of the downtime hours. These records are the plant's own, and they fix the size of the problem the sensors are being asked to solve: the downtime is concentrated in the failure mode that the sensor set addresses. A sensor set for all 260 pumps has been quoted at $456k installed, plus $71k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors reportedly cut downtime by 27%; it should be noted, however, that this figure is the vendor's, it was not measured at this plant, and the plant's downtime may respond by more or by less. The trade-off is therefore a $44k pilot against a $456k installation: the pilot buys a plant measurement of the response, on plant pumps under plant operating patterns, before the larger sum is committed. Spare-part lead times, it should be noted, are unchanged by the sensors, and downtime that waits on parts lies outside what the sensors can recover; the pilot's claim does not extend to it. Overall, the pilot's three months on 18 pumps will provide the evidence base the March decision needs, and the report should state the downtime change on the pilot pumps against the corresponding period in the records.
